summary.impact: Low relevance. A routine property-screening study outside the owner's projects.
summary.what: First-principles study of the halide double perovskite Rb2GeNiCl6 as a magnetic semiconductor, reporting thermoelectric, optical and dielectric properties.
summary.why: To assess lead-free candidates for spintronics, thermoelectrics and optoelectronics.

title: First-principles study of halide double perovskite Rb 2 GeNiCl 6 : a stable magnetic semiconductor for spintronic and thermoelectric applications

abstract: ABSTRACT As the semiconductor industry increasingly pivots toward “More than Moore” and “More Moore” paradigms, heterogeneous integration has emerged as a pivotal strategy for achieving system‐level performance breakthroughs. However, residual stress inherent to the integration of dissimilar materials represents a critical bottleneck, directly threatening the integrity and reliability of these advanced systems. Heteroepitaxy, as a representative example, is inherently constrained by stress accumulation, which limits epilayer thickness, increases threading dislocation density (TDD), and degrades device reliability. Here, we present a strain‐inversion strategy that effectively transfers misfit‐induced stress from the epilayer into the substrate stack. Through co‐designed theoretical modeling and experimental validation, we introduce 4H‐SiC/SiO 2 /polycrystalline‐ceramic‐AlN integrated substrates, and demonstrate metalorganic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) growth of 53‐µm‐thick, stress‐free heteroepitaxial GaN films. The films exhibit outstanding structural quality, with full‐width‐at‐half‐maximum (FWHM) values of x‐ray rocking curve of 83 and 119 arcsec for the (002) and (102) planes, respectively, and a TDD of 5 × 10 7 cm −2 . These results not only set a new thickness record for MOCVD‐grown heteroepitaxial GaN but also achieve crystal quality comparable to state‐of‐the‐art benchmarks. Our approach establishes strain‐inverted epitaxy as a highly promising platform for high‐performance nitride devices and paves the way for producing low‐cost and strain‐free GaN and AlN substrates.

summary.how: Co-designed modeling and experiment; stated results are x-ray rocking curve FWHM of 83 and 119 arcsec for (002) and (102) planes and a threading dislocation density of 5×10^7 cm^-2.
summary.impact: Mostly experimental, but context for the GaN HEMT project: substrate stack and dislocation density affect interface and thermal boundary resistance. Thermal properties of the SiC/SiO2/AlN stack are not stated in the abstract.
summary.what: A strain-inversion strategy using 4H-SiC/SiO2/polycrystalline-ceramic-AlN integrated substrates to grow 53-µm-thick, stress-free GaN films by MOCVD.
summary.why: Residual stress in heteroepitaxy limits epilayer thickness, raises threading dislocation density and degrades reliability.

title: Strain‐Inversion Strategy Enables MOCVD Growth of 53 µm Ultra‐Thick, Stress‐Free, Buffer‐Free III‐Nitride Heteroepitaxial Films

abstract: Uranium dioxide (UO2) undergoes defect formation and microstructural changes under reactor irradiation, making atomic-scale modeling crucial for predicting its long-term thermomechanical performance. In this work, the paramagnetic state of bulk UO2 is simulated using non-spin-polarized density functional theory (DFT) without Hubbard-U corrections to ensure a consistent, computationally tractable reference dataset. To bypass the high cost of direct ab initio molecular dynamics (MD), we developed a Behler–Parrinello high-dimensional neural network potential (HDNNP) optimized with an active-learning framework. The training database was constructed from variable-cell MD trajectories across various temperatures and pressures, calculated using the Quantum ESPRESSO package. The resulting HDNNP achieves outstanding accuracy, yielding energy and force test RMSEs of 1.46×10-4 eV/atom and 8.73×10-3 eV/Å, respectively. Implemented in LAMMPS, the potential accurately predicts the equilibrium lattice parameter and single-crystal elastic constants (C11, C12, C44) of UO2. The predicted elastic constants exhibit excellent agreement with experimental data and DFT+U benchmarks, with relative errors remaining within 2–17%. This highlights the model’s capability to serve as a high-fidelity, computationally efficient surrogate for large-scale simulations of the mechanical behavior of nuclear fuels.

summary.how: Training data come from variable-cell MD trajectories at various temperatures and pressures computed with Quantum ESPRESSO using non-spin-polarized DFT without Hubbard-U. Reported test RMSEs are 1.46e-4 eV/atom (energy) and 8.73e-3 eV/Å (forces); elastic constants agree with experiment and DFT+U within 2-17%.
summary.impact: Low relevance to the projects directly; the active-learning MLIP workflow with LAMMPS is similar to the BAs and InGaAs pipelines, but only elastic constants are validated and no phonon or thermal conductivity results are stated.
summary.what: An active-learning Behler-Parrinello high-dimensional neural network potential (HDNNP) for paramagnetic UO2, implemented in LAMMPS, with exchange-correlation functional screening.
summary.why: Atomic-scale modeling is needed to predict long-term thermomechanical performance of UO2 nuclear fuel under irradiation, while direct ab initio MD is too costly.

title: Exchange–Correlation Functional Screening and Development of a High Dimensional Neural Network Interatomic Potential for UO2
venue: Journal of Nuclear Research and Applications

abstract: We investigate the structural, electronic, and phonon transport properties of GaSe0.5Te0.5 and InSe0.5Te0.5 systems in centrosymmetric (CS) and non-centrosymmetric (NCS) configurations using first-principles calculations combined with Boltzmann transport theory. Structural optimization and stability analysis confirm the feasibility of both configurations. Our results show that crystal symmetry plays a decisive role in governing charge and phonon transport. The centrosymmetric phases exhibit higher carrier mobility, reaching 5407 cm²/Vs for CS-GaSe0.5Te0.5 and 1872 cm²/Vs for CSInSe0.5Te0.5, due to reduced carrier–phonon scattering and more symmetric electronic band dispersion. Interestingly, while both Ga and In-based systems are expected to show superior electrical conductivity due to “conductive network” overlap, the additional antibonding character from In–Te bonds in Insystem may further suppress phonon transport, resulting in reduced lattice thermal conductivity. Additionally, inversion-symmetry breaking in the NCS structures enhances lattice anharmonicity, strengthens phonon scattering, and reduces phonon group velocities, leading to a strong suppression of in-plane lattice thermal conductivity. Moreover, the absence of inversion symmetry in the NCSconfiguration induces Rashba-type spin splitting, which modifies the electronic band structure and enhances the Seebeck coefficient. As a result of this symmetry-driven interplay between electronic and phononic transport, NCS-InSe0.5Te0.5 exhibits the best thermoelectric performance, achieving a maximum ZT of ~2.7 at 600 K. These results highlight symmetry engineering as an effective strategy to optimize thermoelectric efficiency in layered chalcogenide systems.

summary.how: Stated results: inversion-symmetry breaking enhances anharmonicity, strengthens phonon scattering and reduces group velocities, suppressing in-plane lattice thermal conductivity; the NCS-InSe0.5Te0.5 reaches a maximum ZT of about 2.7 at 600 K. Specific codes are not stated in the abstract.

summary.what: First-principles plus Boltzmann transport study of structural, electronic and phonon transport in GaSe0.5Te0.5 and InSe0.5Te0.5 in centrosymmetric and non-centrosymmetric configurations.
summary.why: To test how crystal symmetry governs charge and phonon transport for thermoelectric design in layered chalcogenides.

title: Breaking of inversion symmetry as a design parameter for thermoelectric transport in M Se 0.5 Te 0.5 ( M = Ga , In )

abstract: Two-dimensional semiconductors, such as monolayer MoS 2 , combine a technologically useful band gap with a thickness of three atomic planes. The entire carrier density then lies within a few Å of the surface, which makes them useful as field-effect-transistor channels and as chemically sensitive devices. Device design for MoS 2 needs a transport model whose scattering rates are computed rather than calibrated, whose predictions are tested against experiment, and that spans the scales from electron-phonon coupling to terminal current and sensor response. We present a self-consistent ensemble Monte Carlo (EMC) framework for monolayer MoS 2 built on the ViennaEMC solver, which couples a Boltzmann transport model to Poisson’s equation with degenerate free-carrier statistics. The transport model carries wavevector-dependent acoustic, polar-optical, homopolar and intervalley phonon scattering within and between the K valleys and the spin–orbit-split Q valleys, together with remote substrate phonons, screened charged impurities and surface roughness. Every intrinsic input of the transport model is computed from first principles for this work, namely the band structure of the K and Q valleys, the phonon energies, sound velocities and dielectric response, and the electron-phonon couplings from density-functional perturbation theory matrix elements at 34 explicit phonon wavevectors and from Wannier interpolation with the two-dimensional long-range treatment. The model therefore contains no fitted transport parameter and no coupling taken from another calculation, and its scattering rates are checked against an independent solution of the linearised Boltzmann equation with the same couplings. summary.how: All intrinsic inputs (band structure, phonon energies, dielectric response, electron-phonon couplings from DFPT at 34 explicit phonon wavevectors and from Wannier interpolation with 2D long-range treatment) are computed from first principles with no fitted transport parameter. Scattering rates are checked against a linearised Boltzmann equation solution.

Methodologically a useful reference for linking phonon/e-ph data to device models; no thermal results are stated.
summary.what: A self-consistent ensemble Monte Carlo framework for monolayer MoS2 built on the ViennaEMC solver, coupling Boltzmann transport to Poisson's equation, with the velocity-field result feeding a one-dimensional channel model for FET and gas-sensor response.
summary.why: Device design for MoS2 needs a transport model whose scattering rates are computed rather than calibrated and that spans scales from electron-phonon coupling to terminal current.

title: Multiscale ensemble Monte Carlo of transport and gas sensing in monolayer MoS 2

abstract: Abstract We formulate the thermodynamic core of a quaternionic crystal–glass theory. The orientational variable is an SO(3) rotor q∈SU(2), q∼−q, with coherent amplitude ρ. The rotor stiffness is retained, so disclinations enter as failures of smooth orientational continuation rather than as scalar defects inserted after the fact. A glass is not obtained by integrating out a dilute defect gas, which gives only an ordered-side fugacity correction. The glass basin is instead represented by a second field Φ, defined as the frozen part of the orientational holonomy: the disclination charge threading a loop is the conjugacy class of the loop holonomy in the binary point group H, proliferation of disclinations is the area law of the orientational Wilson loop, and Φ is the Edwards–Anderson amplitude of that holonomy, nonzero only when it is frozen. This separates the glass from a liquid, where the holonomy is equally random but not frozen, and from a defect density, which is nonzero in every phase. We construct a two-field Gibbs functional with competing crystal (ρ̸= 0,Φ = 0) and glass (ρ≃0,Φ ̸= 0) saddles. The order of the transition follows from the quartic coupling matrix: strong positive repulsion between ρand Φ gives a first-order boundary, weaker coupling permits a mixed/frustrated regime. The holonomy charge coincides with the Burgers circulation of the nonaffine displacement field in the torsion sector and differs from it in the curvature sector; in the Riemann–Cartan description of the defect density, disclinations source curvature and dislocations source torsion. The freezing of Φ follows from the rearrangement barrier σws that the functional itself defines. The theory outputs the defect correlation length, the rearrangement barrier and the bulk saddle scale…

summary.how: Theoretical construction of a Gibbs functional with competing saddles; the order of transition follows from the quartic coupling matrix. Numerical results are not stated in the abstract.
summary.impact: Low relevance. Abstract field theory of defects and glass formation, with no phonon or thermal transport link to the reader's projects.
summary.what: Formulates a two-field Gibbs theory of quaternionic orientational order, with a crystal field and a glass field defined as the frozen part of orientational holonomy, treating disclinations and dislocations via curvature and torsion.
summary.why: To describe glass formation and defect condensation with a thermodynamic functional that separates glass from liquid and from defect density.

title: A two-field Gibbs theory of quaternionic orientational order and defect condensation in glass formation

abstract: Phonon-mediated superconductivity in binary transition-metal borides reflects a balance between the metal d-states, metal-boron bonding, and the lattice vibrations that couple to them. Here, we compare P6/mmm TcB2 at 20 GPa with I4/mcm Tc2B and P4/mmm Tc3B at 0 GPa within a first-principles framework. Their mechanical responses differ appreciably: TcB2 is the most rigid under its compressed condition, Tc2B shows the strongest tendency toward ductility, and Tc3B falls between the two. Despite these differences, all three phases remain metallic. The states at the Fermi level are dominated by Tc-4d character, although the extent of Tc-d/B-p mixing varies from one compound to another. Charge redistribution is more directional and B-centered in TcB2, but more delocalized around the Tc network in Tc2B and Tc3B. Inclusion of spin-orbit coupling leaves all three compounds metallic. The optical response remains metallic and electric field polarization dependent, with substantial visible reflectivity and strong ultraviolet absorption. Low-frequency Tc rich vibrations dominate the electron-phonon coupling (EPC). With μ* = 0.10, the Tc values of TcB2, Tc2B, and Tc3B are 24.92, 11.07, and 15.12 K, respectively. Although Tc3B exhibits a higher electronic density of states at the Fermi level, N(EF), TcB2 couples most strongly to EPC-active low-frequency modes, showing that the superconducting hierarchy depends on electronic-phonon matching rather than DOS magnitude alone.

summary.how: DFT-based calculations of electronic structure, spin-orbit coupling, optical response and electron-phonon coupling.
summary.impact: Low relevance. Standard DFT/EPC study of superconducting borides, not thermal transport in the reader's semiconductors or interfaces.
summary.what: First-principles comparison of TcB2 (20 GPa), Tc2B and Tc3B: mechanical, electronic, optical properties and electron-phonon-coupling superconductivity (Tc of 24.92, 11.07 and 15.12 K with μ* = 0.10).
summary.why: Phonon-mediated superconductivity in transition-metal borides depends on the balance of d-states, metal-boron bonding and lattice vibrations.

title: Comparative First-Principles Study of the Physical Properties, Phonon-Mediated Superconductivity and Functional Potential of Technetium-Based Binary Borides TcB2, Tc2B and Tc3B

abstract: We performed a comprehensive Raman spectroscopy study of (Bi1-xSbx)2Te3 (BST-x) compounds, with varying Sb concentration, under ambient and high-pressure conditions. At ambient conditions, the frequency of all observed Raman-active modes (E1g, A11g, E2g, A21g) is blue-shifting with increasing Sb concentration, albeit with varying concentration-dependent rate. Based on these results, we calculated the relative force constants as a function of Sb concentration using a harmonic approximation, which shows a mode-dependent variation. The force constants for the lower frequency Raman modes (E1 g and A11g) remain almost composition-independent, while for the higher-frequency ones a profound softening (E2g) or stiffening (A21g) was determined. From the Raman spectroscopy measurements under high-pressure conditions, the corresponding Grüneisen parameters for the three observed Raman-active modes (A11g, E2g, A21g) as a function of composition were determined by combining them with the previously reported Equation of States and the corresponding bulk modulus B0 of the ambient-conditions R-3m phase. The average Grüneisen parameter exhibits a clear maximum for BST-07. Based on Slack's equation, these results are directly related to the optimal ZT values for this composition. Our study provides a solid framework for connecting composition, lattice dynamics, and thermal-transport behaviour, towards establishing the microscopic origin of thermoelectric optimization in BST compounds.

summary.how: Raman spectroscopy under pressure, equation of state and bulk modulus from earlier reports, Slack's equation.
summary.impact: Mostly experimental with a lattice-dynamics angle; the Grüneisen/anharmonicity data could serve as validation targets for phonon calculations, but it is not tied to a current project.
summary.what: Raman study of (Bi1-xSbx)2Te3 at ambient and high pressure; derives composition-dependent force constants (harmonic approximation) and Grüneisen parameters, with a maximum average Grüneisen parameter at BST-07 linked via Slack's equation to optimal ZT.
summary.why: To connect composition, lattice dynamics and thermal transport and find the microscopic origin of thermoelectric optimization.

title: Lattice dynamics study of (Bi1-xSbx)2Te3 compounds: Comparative compositional study of force constants and Grüneisen parameters

abstract: Abstract Aurivillius phase materials are layered ferroelectrics with high thermal stability (>600 °C) and fatigue resistance, yet their polarization is predominantly in-plane, limiting integration into vertical device architectures relevant to future memory, data storage, and neuromorphic computing concepts. Achieving robust vertical polarization in these systems remains fundamentally challenging because of crystallographic symmetry constraints. Although defects can locally reorient polarization, deterministic control of defect topology through growth-mode engineering remains largely unexplored in layered ferroelectrics. Here, we demonstrate that precise control of nominal precursor loading and oxygen partial pressure during direct liquid injection chemical vapor deposition enables a transition in epitaxial Bi4Ti3O12 thin films from two-dimensional growth to dislocation-mediated, chiral spiral growth. This work introduces growth spirals as a controllable route to engineer defect topology and grain morphology, rather than relying on post-growth or stochastic defect formation. Atomic-resolution microscopy and piezoresponse force microscopy reveal that chiral spiral-mediated morphologies exhibit a 135% higher local vertical piezoresponse amplitude and a reduced local vertical switching bias from ±20 to ±5 V compared with two-dimensional films. High-angle annular dark field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) displacement mapping and density functional theory indicate that out-of-phase boundary defect-associated local structural distortions modify local symmetry, bonding, and strain in a manner consistent with an enhanced out-of-plane polarization component and local vertical electromechanical response. These results establish spiral-driven defect…

summary.how: CVD growth, PFM, HAADF-STEM displacement mapping and DFT.
summary.impact: Low relevance. Mostly experimental growth work with no thermal transport; only a loose link to the BaTiO3 dislocation project through oxide dislocation structure.
summary.what: Shows that tuning precursor loading and oxygen partial pressure in direct liquid injection CVD switches epitaxial Bi4Ti3O12 films from 2D growth to dislocation-mediated chiral spiral growth, with 135% higher local vertical piezoresponse and lower switching bias (from ±20 to ±5 V).
summary.why: Aurivillius ferroelectrics have mainly in-plane polarization, limiting vertical device integration; defect topology control through growth mode is unexplored.

title: Growth-Spiral Control of Defect Topology and Local Vertical Piezoresponse in Bi4Ti3O12 Thin Films

abstract: This work investigates how defect engineering and nanostructuring via severe plastic deformation influence electrical and thermal transport in the high-entropy alloy CrMnFeCoNi. High-pressure torsion (HPT) for up to N = 4 turns produces a hierarchical defect structure, including deformation twins at low strains, dislocations and Lomer-Cottrell locks at intermediate strains, and a high fraction of high-angle grain boundaries at large strains. While hardness naturally increases and saturates at ~520 Hv, both electrical and thermal conductivity exhibit an unusual increase upon HPT processing (from 0.953 MS m-1 and 10.3 W m-1 K-1 after homogenization to 1.003 +- 0.005 MS m-1 and 14.4 W m-1 K-1 after N = 4). Analysis based on the Wiedemann-Franz law indicates a modest increase in electron transport (~5%) and a significant increase in phonon transport (~100%) after HPT processing. The phonon mean free path remains small on the order of 0.6-1.1 nm, and comparison with the Cahill-Pohl model shows that heat transport occurs near the minimum thermal conductivity limit, where vibrational modes are strongly scattered. This suggests that the enhancement in thermal transport is not governed by conventional defect scattering, but it is hypothesized that modifications in atomic-scale disorder, such as deformation-induced short-range ordering, are responsible for this unusual behavior. Specific heat capacity increases after HPT, consistent with stored defect energy. The linear thermal expansion exhibits a non-monotonic behavior, decreasing initially due to internal stresses and relaxation effects, and increasing at higher strains due to grain boundary-induced anharmonicity. These findings highlight the complex interplay between defects, atomic-scale disorder, and nanostructure in…

summary.how: Severe plastic deformation (up to 4 turns), conductivity, specific heat and thermal expansion measurements, Cahill-Pohl comparison; phonon MFP about 0.6-1.1 nm.
summary.impact: Mostly experimental, so low priority. The finding that disorder changes near-minimum-limit transport (hypothesized short-range ordering) is a mechanism a computational study could test, but it is not tied to a current project.
summary.what: Measures electrical and thermal conductivity of CrMnFeCoNi after high-pressure torsion; thermal conductivity rises from 10.3 to 14.4 W/m/K, with Wiedemann-Franz analysis giving about 5% more electron and about 100% more phonon transport.
summary.why: To understand how defects and nanostructuring affect electron and phonon transport in a high-entropy alloy.

title: Unusual increase in electrical and thermal conductivity of severely deformed CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy: Roles of disordering and nanostructuring in electron and phonon transport

abstract: Phase Change Materials (PCMs) are materials of interest for applications in switchable non-volatile memory devices due to their fast phase switching between crystalline and amorphous states, exhibiting high electrical and optical contrasts. The fast crystallization rate of PCMs impedes characterization through conventional methods, necessitating newer avenues of analysis. A previous study of ours demonstrated how modeling the Boson peak, a ubiquitous yet elusive contribution to the low-temperature heat capacity of amorphous solids, could serve as a new avenue. In this work, we investigate the low-temperature heat capacity and the heat flow at elevated temperatures of a greater number of PCMs and chalcogenide GeSeTe glasses. The Boson peaks in the heat capacity of an extended range of PCMs are identified, expanding this hallmark glass feature to these technologically important poor glass formers. While PCMs display no clear difference in Boson peaks from those of conventional chalcogenide glasses, they, as a group, could readily be distinguished when combining their Boson peaks with other properties, such as the glass transition temperature and kinetic fragility. We show that the Boson peaks can be modeled and understood through hybridization or coupling of transverse acoustic phonons with quasi-localized modes. Such a phonon-mode coupling picture can be supported by the correlation between the mean Einstein temperature and the product of the Debye temperature and the cube root of the coefficient of excess modes. These results provide a valuable dataset for understanding Boson peaks and the vibrational and thermodynamic properties of amorphous PCMs, laying the groundwork for investigating how the bonding environment influences their vibrational density of states.

summary.how: Heat capacity and heat flow measurements; correlation of mean Einstein temperature with Debye temperature and excess-mode coefficient.
summary.impact: Low relevance to the current crystalline-semiconductor and interface projects; only a loose link via vibrational modes in disordered systems.
summary.what: Identifies Boson peaks in the low-temperature heat capacity of many phase-change materials and chalcogenide GeSeTe glasses, and models them as hybridization of transverse acoustic phonons with quasi-localized modes.
summary.why: Fast crystallization of PCMs hinders conventional characterization; Boson peaks offer another route and a dataset on vibrational and thermodynamic properties.

title: Boson peaks and thermodynamics of amorphous phase-change materials

abstract: Fast and accurate prediction of adsorption energies is critical for high-throughput computational catalyst screening, existing methods compromise either on evaluation speed (full-graph machine learning potentials) or geometric sensitivity (coordination-based models like the alpha-scheme). Here, we present AdsNet, an equivariant graph neural network that directly predicts adsorption energies in a single forward pass, which operates on a local graph restricted only to adsorbate atoms and its immediate surface neighbors within a cutoff radius. This local graph formulation decouples computational complexity from total system size while encoding continuous geometric features (interatomic distances and directional vectors) enabling sensitivity to subtle variations in local bonding environments. AdsNet adopts a message-passing architecture with scalar and vector node features over multiple interaction layers. Trained on AdsTraj, a dataset of 33,920 density functional theory (DFT) calculated structures spanning 26 transition metals and 6 adsorbates (H*, C*, O*, CO*, OH*, HOCO*), the model achieves an adsorption energy root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 0.032 eV and a force RMSE of 0.047 eV/A. Analytic forces obtained via automatic differentiation enable structure relaxation through a projected gradient descent algorithm with adaptive line search, eliminating entire geometry optimizations. Additionally, AdsNet uniquely decomposes predicted adsorption energies into contributions from individual atoms within the local adsorbate graph - an interpretability feature unattainable with conventional machine-learning potentials. AdsNet thus establishes an accurate, highly efficient, and interpretable framework for large-scale adsorption energy prediction and local interface relaxation…

summary.how: Message passing with scalar and vector features, trained on AdsTraj (33,920 DFT structures, 26 transition metals, 6 adsorbates); relaxation via projected gradient descent with line search.
summary.impact: Low relevance to the thermal projects (catalysis). The atom-wise energy decomposition for interpretability is a mildly interesting idea for MLIP interpretability work.
summary.what: Presents AdsNet, an equivariant GNN predicting adsorption energies in one forward pass from a local graph of the adsorbate and nearby surface atoms (energy RMSE 0.032 eV, force RMSE 0.047 eV/A), with atom-wise energy decomposition.
summary.why: Catalyst screening needs adsorption energy prediction that is fast and geometry-sensitive; full-graph MLIPs are slow and coordination-based models are insensitive.

title: AdsNet: A Graph Neural Network for Direct Adsorption Energy Prediction

abstract: Search for optimal compositions among high-entropy ceramics are challenging due to large composition space, which are unable to test either experimentally or by \textit{ab initio} calculations. Here we present a high-throughput screening for equimolar and non-equimolar high-entropy carbides (HEC) among group IVB and VB transition metals (Ti, Zr, Hf, V, Nb and Ta). Large Atomistic Model MACE, and deep learning based interatomic potential DeePMD trained on \textit{ab initio}-based dataset of structures are used to effectively screen over the thousands of potential non-equimolar compositions among high-entropy carbides of Ti, Zr, Hf, V, Nb and Ta transition metals. A set of both equimolar and non-equimolar HECs are predicted to be stable in order to further synthesize those compositions based on the predictions.

summary.how: MACE and DeePMD potentials screen thousands of compositions; stable candidates are proposed for synthesis. Details of validation are not stated in the abstract.
summary.impact: Moderate-to-low relevance: uses MACE and DeePMD as in the InGaAs project, so it is a practical example of using both for screening, but it targets phase stability rather than thermal transport.
summary.what: High-throughput screening of equimolar and non-equimolar high-entropy carbides of Ti, Zr, Hf, V, Nb and Ta, using the MACE foundation model and DeePMD trained on ab initio data to predict stable compositions.
summary.why: The composition space of high-entropy ceramics is too large to test experimentally or with ab initio calculations.

title: Machine Learning-Driven High-Throughput Screening of Equimolar and Non-Equimolar High-Entropy Carbides

abstract: How chiral phonons survive anharmonic phonon-phonon interactions, which underpin lattice dynamics at finite temperature, remains poorly understood. Using an ab initio many-body approach, we study crystalline tellurium (Te), a strongly anharmonic helical crystal. We show that rotational symmetries in Te impose pseudoangular momentum selection rules on phonon-phonon interactions, restricting mode mixing and scattering at rotationally invariant symmetry points in the Brillouin zone. These symmetries protect the circular polarization of vibrational modes at finite temperature but not their lifetimes such that the dynamic chirality of handed vibrational modes persists to 600 K, even as lifetimes drop sharply. We find that the temperature-dependence of angular momentum generated by a thermal gradient is governed by lifetimes rather than chirality, decreasing by two orders of magnitude between 10 and 600 K.

summary.how: Ab initio anharmonic many-body approach; angular momentum generated by a thermal gradient is shown to be governed by lifetimes rather than chirality (decreasing about two orders of magnitude from 10 to 600 K).
summary.impact: Relevant theory for anharmonic phonon scattering and symmetry selection rules in lattice dynamics (the BTE phonon-property side of the projects) and possibly for the BaTiO3 phonon direction asymmetry work, though the material and focus differ.
summary.what: Ab initio many-body study of chiral phonons in tellurium: rotational symmetries impose pseudoangular-momentum selection rules on phonon-phonon scattering, preserving circular polarization up to 600 K while lifetimes drop sharply.
summary.why: It is poorly understood how chiral phonons survive anharmonic phonon-phonon interactions at finite temperature.

title: Chiral Phonons Protected by Symmetry in a Strongly Anharmonic Helical Material

abstract: The ability to measure thermal properties and visualize heat transport processes with high spatial resolution is becoming increasingly important for materials discovery, next-generation electronics, and advanced manufacturing. As critical dimensions and architectures of novel materials and high performance electronics shrink and become more heterogeneous, thermal transport is no longer governed by bulk material properties alone, but by local variations in microstructure, such as interfaces and defects, while the operating conditions can also play a role. With the development of non-contact pump-probe thermoreflectance techniques, specific heat, thermal conductivity, and interface conductance can be mapped either through wide-field thermos-reflectance images or by scanning technique. However, key challenges remain such as the balance between imaging throughput and measurement accuracy, the extraction of multiple parameters with high confidence, and non-intrusive subsurface characterization, etc. This Review highlights recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI)-assistance in high-throughput data processing, visualizing interfacial thermal transport, and nonintrusive subsurface analysis, and offers outlooks for future research directions such as spectral mapping of heat carriers, three-dimensional property mapping, and AI-agentic experimental designs. We anticipate this Review will motivate future efforts in combining AI with experimental techniques to achieve unprecedented capabilities for thermal characterization of nanoscale materials and device characterization, facilitating materials discovery and electronics revolution.

summary.how: Literature review of pump-probe and wide-field thermoreflectance techniques combined with AI methods.
summary.impact: Useful background for the measurement side of the GaN/Al2O3 interface and HEMT projects (what TDTR-type data may constrain models), and for electronics thermal characterization trends. Experimental/review focus, not a computational method.
summary.what: Review of AI-assisted thermoreflectance imaging: high-throughput data processing, visualization of interfacial thermal transport and nonintrusive subsurface analysis, with outlooks on spectral mapping of heat carriers, 3D property mapping and AI-agentic experimental design.
summary.why: Shrinking, heterogeneous electronics need local mapping of thermal properties, but throughput vs. accuracy and multi-parameter extraction remain challenging.

title: Intelligent Imaging of Thermal Transport in Nanostructures

abstract: First-principles structural relaxation and band calculations require substantial computation and expertise. Here we present Perfumer, a large language model-based agentic framework that couples Quantum ESPRESSO with two predictive models. Across tested structures, pre-relaxation with Perfumer-relax model followed by QE refinement yielded a 2.75-fold overall speedup over QE alone. Perfumer-band model combines a periodic graph neural network with a latent Hermitian spectral head returns 12 band energies at any requested wavevector, preserving reciprocal lattice periodicity and time-reversal symmetry without constructing Hamiltonian. Trained on 125,153 self-curated band structures, Perfumer-band model reaches a median per-material mean absolute error of 0.157 eV on 2,607 test materials, including lanthanide, actinide and magnetic compounds, from held-out composition families spanning 85 elements, taking about 97 ms per material on two consumer CPU cores. The agent turns natural-language requests into relaxation-to-band workflows, from a single uploaded structure to automatically constructed new candidates and returns predicted properties.

summary.how: Agent turns natural-language requests into relaxation-to-band workflows; periodic GNN with latent Hermitian spectral head predicts 12 band energies at any wavevector in about 97 ms on two CPU cores.
summary.impact: Relevant to the interest in agents for automated first-principles workflows; the relax-then-refine pattern could inform automating VASP/phonopy or MLPhonon workflows. It covers electronic bands, not phonons or thermal transport.
summary.what: Presents Perfumer, an LLM-based agentic framework coupling Quantum ESPRESSO with a pre-relaxation model (2.75-fold overall speedup) and a graph-neural-network band predictor (median MAE 0.157 eV on 2,607 test materials, trained on 125,153 band structures).

abstract: Foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials are trained on large, diverse DFT datasets, but their validation rests on equilibrium states, which does not guarantee correct emergent behavior in large-scale molecular dynamics. Where no direct experimental validation is available, comparisons to physically motivated potentials are valuable for drawing insight. We distinguish static properties, which are thermally accessible, from emergent properties, which require work from an external fatigue stress to drive rare events, and compare the potentials on both. An EAM potential and the NequIP foundational potential both agree closely with reference data for many near-equilibrium properties, but NequIP predicts an anomalously low intrinsic stacking fault energy (∼7 times lower than EAM) and thus predicts far more plastic deformation under fatigue cycling of a nanoscale flaw modeled after the classical Griffith crack problem. Per-atom energy distributions after loading show that the two potentials differ most at energies far above what is thermally accessible. We also document memory-related crashes and silent extrapolation as practical concerns for practitioners of these foundational model forms.

summary.how: Fatigue loading of a Griffith-crack-like nanoscale flaw, per-atom energy distributions after loading; also documents memory-related crashes and silent extrapolation.
summary.impact: Relevant to MLIP failure modes across the InGaAs (DeePMD vs MACE), GaN/AlGaN and BAs projects: a reminder that equilibrium accuracy does not ensure far-from-equilibrium reliability, and that silent extrapolation needs checking. Thermal transport is not studied.
summary.what: Compares an EAM potential with the NequIP foundational potential on static and fatigue-driven emergent properties. NequIP predicts an intrinsic stacking fault energy about 7 times lower than EAM and far more plastic deformation under fatigue cycling of a nanoscale crack.
summary.why: Foundational MLIPs are validated on equilibrium states, which does not guarantee correct emergent behavior in large-scale MD.

title: Emergent Fatigue Dynamics from Foundational Interatomic Potentials

abstract: In this work, we investigate thermal transport in a set of thin-film layers used in modern HEMT designs. Our theoretical analysis employs three phonon-transport models of increasing sophistication, ranging from a relatively simple Debye-approximation model to a first-principles framework that incorporates Density Functional Theory (DFT)-derived harmonic and anharmonic phonon properties. To describe ternary semiconductors, alloy scattering is also considered, and to account for the properties of non-ideal, polycrystalline thin films, scattering at grain and film boundaries is taken into account. For modeling the specific samples at hand, the latter are fitted to thermal conductivity data measured with Time-Domain Thermoreflectance (TDTR). Overall, we find that the first-principles model performs best and produces the most physically consistent results. Special emphasis is placed on establishing a reliable procedure for determining intrinsic transport properties dominated by Umklapp scattering. Building on these, it is then possible to systematically add additional scattering terms to the models and assess how model-inherent factors, such as the treatment of scattering rates or the description of the phonon dispersion, affect model accuracy and overall predictive capabilities.

summary.how: Models with DFT harmonic and anharmonic properties, alloy scattering, and boundary scattering fitted to TDTR data; emphasis on a procedure for extracting intrinsic Umklapp-dominated properties.
summary.impact: Directly relevant to the GaN/AlGaN HEMT multiscale thermal modeling project: gives a benchmark of model fidelity (first-principles model performs best) and a procedure for intrinsic vs. extrinsic scattering that could be compared against the MLIP-to-BTE pipeline.

abstract: ABSTRACT BiTe‐based room‐temperature thermoelectric (TE) material family suffers from intrinsic efficiency‐limiting carrier‐mobility trade‐offs. Herein, we report an n‐type Bi 0.75 Sb 0.25 Te 0.7 S 0.15 Se 0.15 material with tailored local compositional fluctuations, which achieves a peak ZT of ∼ 0.64 at 377 K and a record‐high average ZT ave of ∼0.56 over 300–573 K, which stands as the maximum value for BiTe‐based TE systems. The excellent performance originates from conduction band flattening and dense intragranular dislocations, which are produced by the local compositional fluctuations. Band flattening spanning the Γ–A path together with enhanced valleys alignment increase the carrier effective mass, thereby improving the Seebeck coefficient. In addition, intragranular dislocations induce multiscale stress mismatches to achieve efficient phonon scattering, while reducing lattice elastic deformation and weakening phonon‐electron coupling. These synergistic effects allow this alloy a high power factor of ∼14.7 µW cm −1 K −2 and a low lattice thermal conductivity of 0.37 W m −1 K −1 at 377 K. This work proposes a feasible and effective strategy for modulating charge and phonon transport in TE materials.

abstract: Photopolymerization of acrylated epoxidized soybean oil (AESO) is a convenient model of a self-organizing process in a soft, bio-based material: ultraviolet light starts a free-radical chain reaction, the growing network releases heat, and the mobility of molecular groups changes on several time scales at once. We follow this process from two sides. Experimentally, the real and imaginary parts of the dielectric permittivity of an AESO:VDM (1:0.5) mixture with 3 mol% of the photoinitiator DMPA were recorded at 500-5000 Hz under an intermittent on/off illumination protocol, and the resulting time series were analysed with a sliding-window Shannon entropy and the Grassberger-Procaccia correlation integral. Both measures show that short light pulses at the start of curing trigger strongly correlated, collective relaxation, which fades as the network forms, leaving only localized reorientations active. We describe these reorientations as orientational defects and quantify their energetics with the MACE-OFF23 machine learning interatomic potential, using relaxed dihedral scans of five rotational modes (α, α/β, β, γ, δ) of an AESO fragment. Compared with density functional theory (DFT) reference profiles, MACE reproduces the shape of all five profiles (Pearson r=0.95-0.98) and the hierarchy of barriers - from 2.9 eV for the constrained main-chain rotation, through 0.54-0.81 eV for the acrylate rotations, to 0.16-0.18 eV for the methyl and 0.06 eV for the hydroxyl rotation - while underestimating the barrier heights by 3-20%. A simple Arrhenius estimate shows that the acrylate rotations are the modes closest to the frequency window of the dielectric measurement.

abstract: Determining unique atomic coordinates from powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) remains challenging because peak overlap, weak scattering from light elements, limited scattering contrast between elements with similar atomic numbers, and experimental noise render the inverse problem underdetermined. Here, we present XCAPE (XRD-Constrained Accelerated Prediction Engine), a crystal structure prediction (CSP) framework that integrates experimentally derived composition, unit cell parameters, space group, and PXRD data into a symmetry-aware evolutionary search. XCAPE explores Wyckoff-site configurations using tailored mutation operations, evaluates candidates by both energetic stability and diffraction agreement, and accelerates geometry optimization using a universal machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP). The framework recovered 71 of 77 database-derived benchmark structures (92.2%) from simulated PXRD patterns and all 12 reference structures from experimental PXRD patterns. It further identified 12 candidate structure assignments that are consistent with experimental PXRD patterns, lack matching entries in the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD), and are thermodynamically competitive at the MLIP level. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations showed that 10 of these 12 candidates lie within 10 meV/atom of the convex hull. By bridging experimental diffraction data and physically plausible atomistic models, XCAPE can provide structural insight into previously unresolved materials and support accelerated materials discovery in automated research workflows.

abstract: Abstract Two-dimensional materials with high Fermi velocities are promising for high-speed electronic and optoelectronic applications, yet experimental realizations beyond graphene remain scarce. Here, we report the successful synthesis of a triangular monolayer of antimony (Sb) on the wide-gap semiconductor SiC. Using combined angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) in combination with density functional theory (DFT), we reveal substrate-engineered orbital filtering that isolates broad-bandwidth, highly dispersive px and py bands, yielding a compensated Fermi surface with an ultrahigh Fermi velocity surpassing that of pristine graphene. Linear dichroism in ARPES measurements confirms the orbital polarization of the high-velocity bands. Consistent with triangular lattice physics, a valley Dirac cone emerges deep below the Fermi level because of enhanced Sb band filling. These results establish triangular antimonene as a two-dimensional p-orbital metal with consistently high in-plane Fermi velocities across its Fermi level electronic states.

abstract: Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) make atomistic simulations possible at scales beyond the reach of density functional theory (DFT). Matlantis PFP is a uMLIP that treats a variety of domains, including crystals, molecules, and surfaces, with a single model. PFP v8 incorporated a training dataset computed with the r2SCAN functional, chosen for its good agreement with experiment, but the elements and domains covered by that dataset were limited. Here we present Matlantis PFP v9, in which the training data computed with the r2SCAN functional are extended to the lanthanides from Pr to Lu and to the elements from Po to Cm, for a total of 96 elements, and to additional domains such as clusters and adsorption structures. The formation energies of crystals containing the newly supported elements reproduce experimental standard enthalpies of formation with the same level of accuracy as crystals composed only of previously supported elements, and the adsorption energies of molecules on transition-metal surfaces have an overall error against experiment comparable to that of DFT-PBE, although chemisorbed species are overbound. On the same type of GPU (A100), the inference speed and the maximum system size exceed those of SevenNet-Omni, a public uMLIP trained on r2SCAN data: forces are evaluated three to four times faster, and five to ten times as many atoms can be handled. As a result, PFP-R2SCAN is now applicable to systems containing rare-earth and actinide elements and to adsorption on surfaces.

summary.how: Formation energies match experiment as well as for previously supported elements; adsorption energy errors are comparable to DFT-PBE, with chemisorbed species overbound. Forces are 3-4 times faster than SevenNet-Omni on an A100, with 5-10 times larger systems.

abstract: A fundamental challenge in soft matter physics is to describe materials, such as the living cytoplasm and tissues, that are simultaneously active, chemically driven, and exhibit long-lasting memory of mechanical stresses. Here, we construct a generalized hydrodynamic framework at finite wave vectors and frequencies that is applicable to nonequilibrium fluids with memory. By leveraging stationary correlation identities, we derive a generalized linear response theory for nonequilibrium steady states. This framework serves as a formal extension of Onsager’s regression hypothesis beyond thermal equilibrium. Our approach provides a direct pathway to derive transport coefficients from steady-state fluctuations without the traditional Mori-Zwanzig projection-operator formalism, generalizing the Green-Kubo relations to nonequilibrium systems. As a corollary, we derive two model-free variants of the nonequilibrium fluctuation-response relation for non-Markovian dynamics. These generalized relations explicitly capture the nonequilibrium circulating currents—an out-of-equilibrium signature that is invisible to conventional scalar formulations or frameworks that treat degrees of freedom independently. Applying our theory to chemically driven active fluids reveals the emergence of active viscoelastic memory, wherein chemical reaction cycles dynamically renormalize the macroscopic viscous response. Strikingly, this active memory can induce negative storage modulus at finite frequencies, a behavior absent in ordinary viscoelastic fluids. Our first-principles framework rigorously extends linear rheology to nonequilibrium systems and provides a foundation for understanding non-Markovian dynamics across a broad range of biological and synthetic active matter.

abstract: This work analyzes the high-frequency performance constraints of AlGaN/GaN heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs) and proposes a novel band-engineered graded base N-polar AlGaN/GaN HBT and evaluates the RF performances. Unlike conventional p-GaN base designs, we propose a graded base in the N-polar orientation which offers polarization-induced hole accumulation with quasi-electric field-assisted minority carrier transport. The proposed design simultaneously mitigates the longstanding current crowding, Webster effect, and conventional base resistance limitations. Using well-calibrated two-dimensional TCAD simulations, the proposed compositionally graded base HBT projects peak f_T/f_{max} of 190/200 GHz with a power density (V_{br}I_{max}/8 > 20 W/mm), offering a promising pathway toward simultaneous high-frequency and high-power GaN millimeter-wave electronics.

abstract: Abstract Optical skyrmions have been explored predominantly in free-space structured fields, whereas their realization in low-loss dielectric near-field platforms remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate spin–orbit conversion mediated by the spin-redirection Berry phase in a suspended-layer dielectric waveguide of wide-bandgap hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), producing near-field Stokes skyrmions and their symmetry-controlled lattices. Projection onto the rotating TE basis introduces a spin-dependent geometric phase, imprinting orbital angular momentum on the guided field. Under circularly polarized excitation, simulated Stokes-parameter maps reveal near-field optical skyrmions. By further exploiting boundary symmetry, we show that these textures can be reorganized into Meron and hybrid vortex–saddle lattices. The underlying mechanism is supported by photoemission electron microscopy measurements and simulation analysis. This work establishes a dielectric platform for geometric-phase engineering of near-field skyrmions, providing a route toward on-chip topological photonics.

abstract: Abstract SiC as a representative third-generation wide-bandgap semiconductor, is of great importance for high-power electronics, high-frequency devices, and radiation-resistant applications. However, the microscopic mechanisms underlying femtosecond laser-induced nonthermal melting in SiC remain insufficiently understood. Herein, real-time time-dependent density functional theory is employed to investigate the electron dynamics of 4H-SiC under 800 nm femtosecond laser irradiation with intensities ranging from 10 10 to 10 14 W/cm 2 . The ionization mechanisms, energy absorption, current density dynamics and dielectric response are systematically analyzed. As the laser intensity increases, 4H-SiC undergoes a transition from multiphoton absorption (Keldysh parameter γ >> 1) to tunnel ionization ( γ<<1), with a crossover threshold at approximately 5×10 12 W/cm 2 . The phase relationship between the induced current and the electric field evolves from in-phase (dielectric response) to quadrature (Drude metallic response), providing a dynamical signature of photo-induced metallization. Analysis of the density of states difference reveals continuous electron occupation filling in the conduction band and hole deepening in the valence band, culminating in bandgap collapse at intensities exceeding 10 13 W/cm 2 . The nonthermal melting threshold is determined to be approximately 2 eV/atom, corresponding to a laser intensity of approximately 10 13 W/cm 2 . Rate equations are used to estimate the total number of excited electrons and the corresponding plasma frequency, which reaches approximately 12 eV at laser intensity of 10 13 W/cm 2 , consistent with the observed optical breakdown behavior. abstract: Abstract We investigated the effects of Ar and Kr heavy-ion irradiation at 1.0 × 10 7 ions/cm 2 on unbiased AlGaN/GaN high-electron-mobility-transistors. After irradiation, the drain current and transconductance degraded by less than 10 %, and the threshold voltage shifted slightly for both ions. In contrast, Kr-irradiated HEMTs exhibited much degradation in gate leakage current and off-state breakdown voltage than Ar-irradiated devices, which is attributed to Schottky contact deterioration and defect generation in the AlGaN barrier. SRIM simulations revealed that Kr ions generate more vacancies throughout the HEMT layer than Ar ions owing to larger nuclear energy loss, consistent with these results.

abstract: We perform molecular dynamics simulations of molten Lithium Fluoride, comparing the classical Buckingham and Born-Huggins-Mayer potentials with machine-learnt interatomic potentials - the MACE-MP-0b3 (small) foundation model potential, and a fine-tuned version thereof. We find that the MACE-MP-0b3, out-of-the-box, is able to accurately reproduce the experimental shear viscosity across the liquid state comparable with polarisable potentials despite not itself being polarisable. Previous viscosities computed using classical potentials are under-predicted, which has previously been attributed to a suppressed melting temperature. Prompted by this we compare the melting points of these potentials. We find that the machine-learnt potentials address the significant underestimation of the melting point of the classical potentials, though the refined potential and the foundation model differ significantly between themselves. We probe the microscopic structure and dynamics of each model to further elucidate the considerable change in viscosity between classical and machine-learnt potentials. We find that, despite their lower melting temperature, classical potentials produce considerably stiffer, higher frequency, single-particle and collective charge-transport dynamics on account of their fixed charges. However, in the long-wavelength limit, the many-body machine-learnt potentials feature more elastic collective motion that governs the diffusion of momentum and is therefore responsible for the enhanced shear viscosity.

summary.how: Out-of-the-box MACE-MP-0b3 reproduces experimental shear viscosity and raises the melting point, though the fine-tuned and foundation models differ markedly. The microscopic analysis shows more elastic long-wavelength collective motion in the MLIPs.

abstract: Coherent interfacial energies govern the formation and evolution of multiphase microstructures, but their calculation is complicated by the elastic energy required to accommodate lattice mismatch. Here, we construct a high-throughput DFT database of 365 coherent FCC/FCC, BCC/BCC, and HCP/HCP interfaces involving 41 metallic elements and lattice mismatches of up to 25%. We use the supercell approach, consisting of constructing superlattices of different thicknesses to separate the coherency strain energy from the chemical contribution to the interfacial energy. We classify the results according to the long-range ordering tendency of each binary system and the sign of the calculated interfacial energy. Most phase-separating systems exhibit positive interfacial energies, whereas most compound-ordering systems exhibit negative values, reflecting favorable unlike-atom bonding. Exceptions show that the chemical preference at a particular interface need not coincide with bulk phase behavior: coherency strain can oppose ordering, and stable compounds can adopt structures distinct from the calculated superlattices. No clear correlation of interfacial energy with lattice mismatch is observed, whereas coherency strain energy increases with mismatch. For phase-separating systems, the lowest interfacial energies generally occur along the closest-packed orientations, while this trend is absent for ordering systems. Comparisons with reported interfacial energies and binary phase diagrams show qualitative consistency, although quantitative agreement varies with reference states, structural constraints, and temperature. The database provides a systematic reference for metallic coherent heterophase interfaces and demonstrates the importance of separating strain and chemical energy…

abstract: In the rapidly evolving field of machine learning (ML) for atomistic simulations of materials and molecules, achieving transferability across different systems remains a key challenge. In this contribution, we demonstrate a case of transfer learning in which an ML model trained exclusively on surface slab data of the cubic ( α ) phase of CsPbI 3 perovskite can reproduce the key features of the dynamic behavior for different phases of the bulk material. Using an equivariant message-passing network (MACE) architecture, we construct an efficient ML force field trained on a dataset obtained from molecular dynamics simulations of a CsPbI 3 slab. The resulting model yields stable and reliable trajectories for both slab and bulk, reproducing the experimentally observed phase transitions of CsPbI 3 . We demonstrate that pairwise dispersion methods (TS/D3) mispredict the correct phase of CsPbI 3 bulk at ambient conditions, while more advanced approaches (MBD-NL/rVV10) recover both the experimentally observed phase sequence with increasing temperature (orthorhombic–tetragonal–cubic) and the corresponding phase-transition temperatures. Through a local analysis of the rotational driving forces acting on PbI 6 octahedra, we show that this discrepancy can be traced to the strong sensitivity of Cs and I atomic forces to the treatment of van der Waals (vdW) dispersion. Overall, our results demonstrate that surface–slab datasets augmented with an accurate treatment of vdW dispersion provide a robust foundation for constructing transferable machine-learning force fields that consistently describe both surface and bulk behavior across multiple length scales.

abstract: Molybdenum sulfides are in the spotlight of materials science thanks to their interesting properties for applications in optoelectronics, nanocomposites, lubricants, and catalysis. The structural characterization of Molybdenum sulfides is a crucial step to understand and tune their properties. Vibrational techniques, such as infrared and Raman spectroscopy, can directly link to structural features, but the experimental literature suffers from large variability. Theoretical calculations are a powerful tool complementing and explaining empirical measurements. The reliability of first-principles calculation depends on the level of approximation made, taking into account disorder, doping, or temperature to yield a good description of the phonon statistics and related measurable quantities, such as the infrared and Raman peaks. In this study we calculate the Raman spectrum of crystalline 2H-MoS2, including broadening and shifts due to thermal and anharmonic effects. Our results demonstrate excellent agreement with experimental measurements; notably, the calculated temperature trends in frequencies and linewidths align with empirical observations. These findings establish a robust computational framework, paving the way for similar studies on amorphous Molybdenum sulfides.

abstract: Traditional crystalline silicon photovoltaic modules employ irreversible laminated packaging. Once individual cells fail or become obstructed, the entire string’s output power declines significantly, and repairs cannot be made without damaging the module—this constitutes a fundamental limitation of “static packaging.” This paper proposes a cell-level dynamic reconfigurable photovoltaic architecture that encapsulates each cell as a standardized “power generation cell,” integrating chip-level power optimizers, microfluidic active cooling systems, and high-speed industrial communication networks. Through a matrix backplate, the system enables online hot-swapping of cells and millisecond-scale electrical reconfiguration. This architecture redefines photovoltaic systems from static “power panels” into self-healing energy networks with physically maintainable components and software-defined energy pathways. A joint electrical-informatics-reliability simulation model was developed, comparing the proposed architecture with traditional modules under local failures, non-uniform shading, and long-term degradation conditions using Python simulations. Results demonstrate that during single-cell failure, the proposed architecture isolates the faulty cell and switches to backup cells within 5 ms, achieving power loss below 2%; over a 25-year lifecycle, the system’s rated output availability approaches 100%, whereas traditional modules show annual declines to approximately 82%. Active liquid cooling maintains cell temperatures at 45 ± 2 °C, thereby substantially reducing thermal hotspot risks under the simulated conditions. abstract: The ground-state structures of fifteen free-standing [111]-oriented ferroelectric superlattices (SLs) based on perovskite oxides and involving a single-atom substitution---BaTiO₃/SrTiO₃, PbTiO₃/SrTiO₃, PbTiO₃/PbZrO₃, SrZrO₃/SrTiO₃, PbZrO₃/BaZrO₃, BaTiO₃/BaZrO₃, PbTiO₃/BaTiO₃, BaTiO₃/CaTiO₃, KNbO₃/KTaO₃, KNbO₃/NaNbO₃, SrTiO₃/SrHfO₃, BaTiO₃/BaSnO₃, PbTiO₃/CaTiO₃, SrTiO₃/CaTiO₃, and PbZrO₃/SrZrO₃---are calculated from first principles. It is shown that in eleven considered SLs the ground state is ferroelectric. A distinctive feature of the structure of the superlattices is that both the ferroelectric distortions and the distortions associated with octahedral rotations are described by phonons at the Γ~point of the Brillouin zone. The importance of taking into account structural distortions associated with octahedral rotations, which in some cases lead to significant changes in the ferroelectric properties of SLs, is demonstrated. The thermodynamic stability of superlattices grown in the [111] and [100] directions is compared. An analysis of the force constants of the superlattices helps to explain the peculiarities of the ferroelectric properties of the superlattices and the corresponding solid solutions.

summary.how: DFT ground-state structures, with Γ-point phonon analysis of distortions and force-constant analysis; compares [111] and [100] growth stability.
summary.impact: Low relevance. It covers BaTiO₃/SrTiO₃ systems but addresses ferroelectricity, not thermal transport; only the force-constant analysis is loosely related to the BaTiO₃/SrTiO₃ projects.

summary.why: To understand how ferroelectric distortions and octahedral rotations together determine superlattice properties.

title: Properties of [111]-oriented ferroelectric superlattices based on oxides with a perovskite structure

abstract: Thermoelectric materials realize direct heat–electricity conversion and hold great promise for waste heat recovery. Maximizing the figure of merit [Formula: see text] requires decoupling the interdependent Seebeck coefficient, electrical conductivity and thermal conductivity. This review surveys recent advances across conventional inorganic systems (Heusler alloys, skutterudites, Zintl phases, perovskites, chalcogenides, fluorite/antifluorite), two-dimensional layered materials, organic composites and topological insulators, highlighting that prominent [Formula: see text] breakthroughs arise from matching effective modulation strategies to specific material systems. Strategies for suppressing lattice thermal conductivity [Formula: see text] — intrinsic anharmonicity, hierarchical defect engineering and multiphase heterointerfaces — are analyzed, alongside emerging mechanisms of four-phonon scattering, wave-like phonon tunneling and machine-learning-accelerated calculations. Power factor optimization via band convergence, flat–dispersive band coexistence, spin–orbit coupling modulation and device-level modulation doping is reviewed. Current challenges and future directions are outlined, emphasizing the urgency of bridging computational predictions with experimental realization, developing universal physics-informed descriptors and advancing flexible wide-temperature thermoelectric devices toward practical applications.

abstract: SrTiO 3 is a prototypical perovskite oxide with unique properties that have enabled its use in a wide range of applications, ranging from substrates to photovoltaics. Defects play a key role in the functional properties of SrTiO 3 . In particular, dislocations, i.e., one-dimensional crystal imperfections, can drastically alter structural and electrical properties in their vicinity. In this work, we present a density functional theory study of the effects of dislocations on SrTiO 3 . We find that dislocations introduce strong structural distortions with localized strain values reaching 0.17. As a consequence, nonpolar SrTiO 3 becomes polar, with polarization values up to 46 µ C / cm 2 , exceeding those of some polar perovskites. Dislocations also interrupt the periodic lattice arrangement, leading to phonon modes between 600 cm − 1 and 1000 cm − 1 . In terms of electrical properties, dislocations reduce the bandgap by smearing oxygen 2 p and titanium 3 d states. A Bader charge analysis reveals that free charge carriers accumulate in the heavily distorted regions around the dislocation cores. Overall, the system studied here provides a framework for understanding the key structural and electrical properties of dislocations.

summary.how: Density functional theory on dislocation cells with Bader charge analysis.
summary.impact: Relevant to the BaTiO₃ dislocation and SrTiO₃ grain-boundary projects: the dislocation-core localized phonon modes are a direct comparison point, although thermal conductivity is not computed.

summary.why: Dislocations strongly alter structural and electrical properties of SrTiO₃, a prototypical perovskite.

title: Ab initio study of structural and electrical properties of SrTiO 3 dislocations

abstract: Abstract Bi2Te3-based alloys, particularly (Bi1–xSbx)2Te3, remain the most effective thermoelectric materials near room temperature. In this work, we employ neuroevolution interatomic potentials trained on first-principles data to perform large-scale atomistic simulations of (Bi1–xSbx)2Te3 across a wide range of compositions. The developed potential enables accurate and efficient evaluation of structural stability, phonon transport, and thermoelectric-relevant properties in disordered systems. The potential model reproduces ab initio elastic constants, phonon dispersions, and equilibrium lattice parameters. With the help of molecular dynamics-based dynamic tensile simulations, we show the existence of a factor-of-two anisotropy for the Young’s modulus between in-plane and cross-plane loading directions across the entire composition range. The lattice thermal conductivity across different compositions of (Bi1–xSbx)2Te3 follows the Klemens-type alloy-scattering model, whose values nearly match the experimental results. Our results reveal that alloying-induced atomic disorder plays a dominant role in suppressing lattice thermal conductivity through enhanced phonon scattering, with a non-linear dependence on Sb concentration arising from the competition between mass-disorder scattering and changes in phonon dispersion. We show pronounced anisotropy for in-plane and cross-plane thermal conductivity values in Bi1.08Sb0.92Te3, which has a minimum bulk-average thermal conductivity at 300 K across all compositions. We also develop an MD-assisted model to calculate bipolar thermal conductivity in Bi0.4Sb1.6Te3, which can be extended to any alloy composition. Finally, the transferability of the NEP model is explored with the help of interfacial thermal transport between Bi2Te3…

Alloy κ follows a Klemens-type model and nearly matches experiment. Transferability is tested on interfacial transport between Bi2Te3 and a second material (abstract truncated).

title: Atomistic Study of Alloying Effects in (Bi1– x Sb x )2Te3 Thermoelectric Materials Using Neuroevolution Potentials

abstract: Modern equivariant machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have dramatically improved the accuracy of and the scales accessible to atomistic simulation, yet the thermodynamic sampling methods needed to turn those potentials into finite-temperature phase stability predictions have not kept pace computationally. We present the GPU-native, massively parallel nested sampling framework JAXRENS, implemented on top of JAX, which removes the practical bottlenecks preventing atomistic nested sampling from being combined with state-of-the-art MLIPs. The framework provides distributed multi-GPU execution, vectorised ensembles of walkers, and direct interoperability with modern force fields. We demonstrate the highly beneficial scaling of JAXRENS on hardware accelerators, and apply it to the simulation of the ZnS phase diagram based on a MACE foundation model, a procedure previously computationally inaccessible. Despite requiring in the order of 10^10 model evaluations, the final converged simulation completed within six days on four GPUs, marking an important step towards routine, first-principles-quality predictions of finite-temperature phase stability using machine-learned interatomic potentials.

summary.how: Vectorised walker ensembles and distributed multi-GPU execution; the converged ZnS run needed about 10^10 model evaluations and finished in six days on four GPUs.
